analysis.one_liner: Lets victims of AI-generated fake sexual images sue the people who made or shared them.
analysis.headline: Despite 14 bipartisan cosponsors, the bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a vote by the full House before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would give victims of non-consensual intimate images — including AI-generated 'deepfakes' that look real — the right to sue in federal court. A victim could recover $150,000 in damages or their actual losses, plus lawyer's fees, and a judge could order the images taken down. It would also let victims file under a pseudonym so their name stays out of public records, and they would have up to 10 years after discovering the fake (or after turning 18) to sue.
analysis.who_benefits: Victims of non-consensual intimate images, a group that is overwhelmingly women and girls, gain a federal right to sue. Under current law it is hard to hold the creators and sharers of AI 'deepfake' pornography accountable, because the images are not real and many state laws predate the technology. This bill would let victims recover substantial money damages, get court orders forcing images offline, sue anonymously to avoid further exposure, and make the person who harmed them pay their legal bills. It would cover both fakes and real images shared without consent.

how_it_helps.text: It creates a federal civil lawsuit for victims of 'digital forgeries' — AI-generated or altered intimate images of an identifiable person that look real — letting them sue anyone who knowingly produced, possessed with intent to share, shared, or solicited the fake without consent.
Victims could collect $150,000 in damages (or their actual damages) plus attorney's fees and court costs, and courts could order the images taken down by injunction.
It lets victims file under a pseudonym and keep their personal information sealed, and gives them up to 10 years after discovering the fake (or turning 18) to sue.
It covers disclosure, solicitation, and possession of non-consensual real intimate images too, and explicitly leaves stronger state laws in place.

analysis.who_pays: People who knowingly create, possess for sharing, share, or solicit non-consensual intimate images or AI deepfakes, and websites or distributors of that content, bear the cost: civil judgments of up to $150,000 per violation, plus attorney's fees and court orders to remove the images.
analysis.who_pays_short: Creators and sharers of intimate deepfakes

drawbacks.text: A civil lawsuit is an expensive remedy. Victims would need to identify anonymous perpetrators, hire a lawyer, and litigate — and the strongest cases would tend to belong to people who can afford the fight, even with attorney's fees recoverable.

The bill's definition of a 'digital forgery' is broad — any AI-made intimate image of an identifiable person that seems indistinguishable from real, even if labeled fake — and defendants would argue this could sweep in parody, satire, or altered images that are not truly sexual, raising free-speech concerns.
Liquidated damages of $150,000 per violation, available without proving actual harm, could pressure settlements in borderline cases and give well-resourced plaintiffs leverage in litigation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — a real federal remedy, including money damages and court orders to take images down, for people whose likeness is used in fake sexual images — is substantial and targeted at conduct almost no one defends. The main costs are real but manageable: defendants could argue the "digital forgery" definition is broad enough to reach parody or altered images that are not truly sexual, and $150,000 in automatic damages could pressure settlements in close cases. The bigger honest caveat is on the delivery side: a civil suit costs money and requires finding an anonymous perpetrator, so the remedy would work best for victims with resources and fail many others. Compared with that gap, the bill's protections for pseudonymous filing and its preservation of stronger state laws are sensible design features.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the two-year Congress expired, so it died without any vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 6, 2024 and referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
The action history shows no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action for the rest of the 118th Congress, which ended January 3, 2025.

The bill never came to any vote, so its protections for victims of non-consensual intimate deepfakes — including $150,000 damages, court orders to remove images, and pseudonymous filing — never became law in that Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who create and share non-consensual AI sexual imagery, and sites that profit from distributing it, are better off: no new federal civil liability was created. Victims gained nothing from this Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Creators and distributors of deepfake pornography

for.name: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create a federal civil cause of action for victims of non-consensual intimate deepfakes.

for.name: Mike Garcia
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor, giving the bill bipartisan backing from the day of introduction.

for.role: Members of the House (with Democratic cosponsors Raskin, Ross, Lieu, Wexton, and Ross)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors, bringing the bill to 14 cosponsors split evenly between 7 Republicans and 7 Democrats.

against.name: House Committee on the Judiciary
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Jim Jordan (R-OH)
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — for the remaining ten months of the 118th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's cosponsorship was evenly split — 7 Republicans and 7 Democrats signed on — and its original cosponsor list included five Republicans; the bill died from committee inaction, not from a party-line vote.

industries.note: Tools that let users create realistic fake sexual images of real people expose their operators and users to federal lawsuits for $150,000 per violation. Some of this content is a paying business built on non-consensual imagery.

The bill's liability reaches people who knowingly disclose or solicit these images, which could reach platforms in some circumstances, though it focuses on producers and sharers rather than host liability. Platforms that profit from viral non-consensual content benefit from the bill's death.
